item.title: Wastewater blower VFD: why energy savings erode
item.description: Dissolved oxygen sensor drift silently reverses VFD energy savings at wastewater plants. Three historian patterns reveal the cause, and the fix starts with calibration records.
item.content:encoded:
Variable frequency drives on aeration blowers are among the most reliable energy investments a wastewater plant can make. The engineering is sound: slow the blower when oxygen demand drops, and power consumption falls by the cube of the speed reduction. Many plants documented 15 to 25 percent reductions in blower energy in the months after commissioning. Not all of them still see those numbers.

The most common reason is not a failing drive, a degraded motor, or the wrong control strategy. It is the dissolved oxygen sensor feeding the control loop.

Quotable insight: A blower VFD can only be as efficient as the measurement telling it when to slow down. If that sensor reads low, the controller drives blowers harder, and the savings disappear into electricity you cannot account for.

How VFD DO control is supposed to work

In a properly functioning aeration control loop, a dissolved oxygen sensor reports basin concentration to a controller. The controller compares that reading to a setpoint, typically 1.5 to 2.5 mg/L for activated sludge, and adjusts blower output through one or more variable frequency drives. When influent load drops overnight, demand-based control backs the blowers off. When load rises in the morning, blowers ramp back up.

The energy arithmetic behind this is centrifugal fan physics. For a multi-stage centrifugal or turbo blower, power consumption scales with the cube of rotational speed. A blower running at 80 percent of design speed uses approximately 51 percent of design power. At 90 percent of design speed, it uses approximately 73 percent. The difference between those two operating points, 22 percentage points of rated power, is what demand-based control captures when it works as designed.

The Florida Water and Pollution Control Operators Association published analysis in April 2026 showing that demand-based DO control typically reduces blower energy by 10 to 25 percent at secondary treatment plants, and that PLC-optimized control can reach 20 to 40 percent. (FWPCOA, "Demand-Based DO Control And Energy Optimization," April 2026) Those ranges describe what the control system saves when the sensor is providing an accurate signal.

The sensor drift that quietly reverses it

Dissolved oxygen sensors in mixed liquor face a relentless fouling environment. Biofilm builds on membrane-covered electrochemical sensors and on the optical surfaces of luminescent sensors. Suspended solids accumulate on probe housings. The most common consequence of fouling is a reading that drifts low: the deposit impedes diffusion or light transmission, and the sensor reports less oxygen than is actually present.

A sensor reading 1.4 mg/L when the basin contains 2.1 mg/L presents the controller with a problem that does not exist. The basin is already 0.6 mg/L above setpoint. The controller sees it 0.1 mg/L below setpoint and commands higher blower output. The VFD speeds up. Over-aeration begins, and it is completely silent: no alarms fire, the historian records the sensor value as if it were accurate, and the control loop looks like it is working.

The result is a system where the VFD is still installed, the control loop is still active, and the blowers are running harder than the process needs. The savings documented at commissioning, when the sensors were freshly calibrated, erode as sensor bias accumulates between calibration events.

What the cost of eroded savings looks like

The U.S. EPA benchmarks secondary treatment activated sludge plants at approximately 1,500 kWh per million gallons for electricity consumption, with aeration systems representing 50 to 75 percent of that total. (U.S. EPA, Ensuring a Sustainable Future: An Energy Management Guidebook for Wastewater and Water Utilities) The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported the national average industrial electricity rate at $0.0977 per kWh in July 2026. (EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026)

Modelled example for a 10 MGD secondary treatment plant:

Annual aeration energy at benchmark3,285,000 kWh/yr
Aeration electricity cost at $0.098/kWh~$322,000/yr
Savings at commissioning (20%, demand-based control)~$64,000/yr
Savings after 18 months of sensor drift (reduced to ~8%)~$26,000/yr
Annual value of eroded savings~$38,000/yr

This is a modelled example using published benchmarks and illustrative drift-induced savings erosion. Actual figures depend on load profile, treatment configuration, calibration schedule, and utility tariff. A plant running at higher flow or with older blowers will see larger absolute numbers. A plant with weekly calibration will see less erosion.

The point of the table is the ratio: the cost of sensor drift that is invisible on the dashboard can exceed the annual maintenance budget for the sensors causing it.

Three patterns that appear in the historian

When VFD savings have eroded due to sensor drift, three patterns tend to appear in historical process data. None of them requires new instrumentation to find.

Blowers at sustained high output during low-demand periods. A functioning demand-based control system should show measurable blower turndown overnight and on weekends, when influent flow and biological oxygen demand are lower. If the historian shows blowers running at 85 percent or higher during those periods, either the setpoint is configured too aggressively or the sensors are overreporting the oxygen deficit.

Step changes in blower output immediately after calibration events. When a sensor has drifted low by 0.5 to 1.0 mg/L and is then recalibrated to the correct value, the control loop sees an immediate improvement and commands lower blower output. That step down shows up in the historian. Its size reveals how far the sensor had drifted, and how long the plant was paying for that drift since the last calibration. A plant running monthly calibration on a sensor that drifts 0.5 mg/L in three weeks has paid for that drift for three weeks before the correction.

Divergent blower output across parallel basins. At plants with multiple aeration basins drawing from a common air header, sensors in different basins drift at different rates depending on local solids loading and maintenance consistency. When two basins receive similar influent loads but their blower outputs differ by 20 percent or more, the most common cause is a measurement offset in one of the sensors. The control loop is faithfully responding to what the sensors report. What the sensors report has diverged from reality.

We documented this exact pattern in 25 days of historian data from an operating plant: one basin was running its blower at more than three times the DO level of its parallel twin, with the blower pinned at maximum output for the full duration of the record. Both basins drew from the same air header. The control loop was functioning. The deviation was worth $3,316 per year in direct blower power, and it was invisible without comparing basins side by side at hourly resolution.

The mechanics of parallel equipment drift in aeration systems, and why the gap tends to grow rather than self-correct, are covered in why parallel equipment drifts apart and what the gap costs.

The calibration interval question

There is no universal answer for how often a DO sensor in activated sludge service should be calibrated. Manufacturer recommendations typically range from weekly to monthly. Actual calibration frequency at operating plants varies considerably, and some plants rely on grab samples and visual inspection rather than a fixed interval.

What determines the right interval is the sensor's actual drift rate in your mixed liquor at your current solids loading. A sensor that drifts 0.1 mg/L per week and holds that drift until the membrane is replaced needs a different schedule than one that degrades faster. The only way to know which situation you are in is to compare sensor readings against a calibrated handheld reference at intervals shorter than your current calibration cycle, not just immediately after calibration.

A calibration-versus-drift log, built from a few weeks of parallel readings, makes the calibration interval decision quantitative rather than a guess based on manufacturer defaults. We examine this approach in detail in DO sensor calibration intervals in activated sludge, including how to build a drift profile and what a typical profile looks like in activated sludge service.

For plants running intermittent aeration for simultaneous nitrification and denitrification, the stakes around calibration intervals are higher. That control strategy uses precise DO swings through the nitrification setpoint to cycle between aerobic and anoxic conditions. A sensor with a standing offset of 0.5 mg/L can shift the timing of those swings in ways that reduce nitrogen removal efficiency and create compliance risk, entirely apart from the energy cost.

Three questions before adjusting the control strategy

When blower energy costs are higher than expected, or when early savings have faded, the instinct is to revisit the control logic: adjust setpoints, tune PID parameters, upgrade the control software. That work sometimes helps. It often does not, because the problem is not the strategy but the measurement feeding it.

Before changing anything in the control loop, three questions are worth answering directly from historian and calibration records.

How large were the step changes in blower output after the last three calibration events? If each calibration produces a visible step down in blower output, the sensor has been reading low between calibration cycles. The step size tells you how much the drift cost.

Do parallel basins show divergent blower outputs during similar load periods? Persistent divergence with no other explanation almost always traces to a sensor offset. It will not resolve with setpoint adjustments.

When was the last time sensor readings were verified against a calibrated handheld at midday, not just immediately after calibration? Sensors that look fine at calibration can drift substantially before the next service event. A midday check, two weeks after calibration, shows whether the reading is holding.

None of this analysis requires hardware beyond what most plants already have. The data is usually in the historian. The constraint is having a way to examine it at the right resolution, across basins, over a window long enough to see the patterns clearly.

If your plant installed blower VFDs with projected savings that have not materialized, or savings that were real initially and have since faded, the measurement quality question is the right place to start. An initial review of historian data from your aeration system can show whether the control loop is working from accurate inputs and where the largest gaps are.

item.title: DO sensor calibration intervals in activated sludge
item.description: DO sensor calibration intervals in activated sludge should match your process fouling rate, not the manufacturer default. Here is the historian method.
item.content:encoded:
Most wastewater plant SOPs specify dissolved oxygen sensor calibration intervals based on the manufacturer's recommendation. For polarographic membrane sensors in aeration basins, that is typically every two to four weeks. For optical (luminescent) sensors, manufacturers often suggest every one to three months.

These intervals are reasonable starting points but not optimized schedules. Manufacturer recommendations are set to cover the demanding end of the range of applications, which in wastewater means high-MLSS activated sludge with aggressive fouling conditions. If your specific process fouls sensors faster, a monthly schedule runs the risk that your aeration control is operating on significantly drifted data for the last two weeks of each cycle. If your process fouls sensors more slowly, a two-week schedule means extra calibration events with no benefit to process control and real costs in technician time and recalibration-induced step changes.

The relevant question for a wastewater plant operator is not "what does the manufacturer recommend?" but "what is the drift rate of this sensor in this basin, and how long can I run before that drift materially affects my aeration control?"

What DO calibration is actually doing

A DO calibration does one thing: it resets the working baseline that your aeration control loop uses to make decisions. During the calibration event, the sensor output is adjusted to match a known reference, typically a two-point calibration against air-saturated water and a zero-oxygen reference. After calibration, the sensor is reading accurately.

Between calibration events, the sensor output drifts. Drift has two main sources: membrane fouling and electrolyte depletion (polarographic), or optical cap fouling and fluorescent dye degradation (luminescent). In both cases, the sensor reads lower than the actual dissolved oxygen concentration as fouling accumulates.

For aeration control, this matters because the blower or diffuser system is responding to the sensor output, not to the actual dissolved oxygen in the basin. A sensor reading 0.8 mg/L when the actual concentration is 1.4 mg/L will hold the blowers on long past the point where the setpoint was met. The basin gets over-aerated. Energy is wasted -- the full cost structure of blower energy at wastewater plants is covered in wastewater aeration energy: cost and the measurement gap. In an intermittent aeration system used for nitrogen removal, the aerobic phase extends, the anoxic fraction shrinks, and denitrification efficiency drops -- the quantified cost of that shift is covered in intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal: what DO sensor precision actually controls. (EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual, 2010, Section 5)

Fouling rates vary by process

Fouling in activated sludge aeration basins is driven primarily by biofilm accumulation on sensor surfaces and entrapment of suspended solids. Both are functions of mixed liquor suspended solids concentration, hydraulic conditions at the sensor location, and aeration intensity.

A sensor positioned directly in a high-turbulence zone of a high-MLSS basin will foul faster than one in a lower-flow zone of a more lightly loaded tank. Optical sensors tend to accumulate a thin biofilm on the luminescent cap that polarographic sensors do not, but they are also not subject to membrane rupture or electrolyte exhaustion. Neither technology eliminates drift; both require calibration at intervals matched to the process.

Standard Methods 4500-O G, which covers the membrane electrode method for dissolved oxygen measurement, recommends calibration whenever "the readings are questioned, when samples of unusual character are analyzed, when temperature changes are sudden, or when the probe is relocated." (Standard Methods for the Examination of Water and Wastewater, 23rd edition, 4500-O G) This is a performance-based standard: calibrate when there is reason to believe the reading has drifted, not on a fixed schedule alone. For a continuous in-line sensor in an aeration basin, that translates to understanding when your process typically produces readings you should question.

Using historian data to calibrate your calibration schedule

Every time a sensor is calibrated in the field, the technician records the pre-calibration reading and the reference value. If your SCADA historian preserves this data, you have a direct record of how far the sensor drifted from each post-calibration baseline to the next pre-calibration check.

Pulling this data over 12 months and plotting cumulative drift against days since last calibration produces a process-specific drift curve for each sensor location. The curve tells you two things: how fast your sensors typically drift, and whether drift is linear (consistent fouling) or step-function (fouling event, usually a process upset or loading change).

For a plant targeting a DO setpoint of 2.0 mg/L with a control band of 0.5 mg/L, the calibration interval should be set so that expected drift at the end of the cycle stays within a fraction of that tolerance. If your drift curve shows 0.3 mg/L per week, a four-week interval means you could be running with a 1.2 mg/L offset by the end of the cycle. That is enough to hold blowers at full speed when the basin is already adequately aerated, or to trigger alarms that reflect sensor state rather than process state.

At an industrial rate of $0.0977/kWh (EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026) and a typical blower draw of 150 kW, one extra hour of unnecessary aeration per day costs approximately $5.34, or roughly $1,950 per year. Across multiple basins with independent sensors, the cumulative cost of operating with drifted DO data is not trivial.

Modelled example: drift cost at two calibration intervals

2-week calibration cycle6-week calibration cycle
Assumed drift rate0.2 mg/L per week0.2 mg/L per week
Max offset at end of cycle0.4 mg/L1.2 mg/L
Estimated excess blower runtimeLowSubstantial
Annual cost (modelled, 150 kW blower)Approx. $500Approx. $3,200

These are modelled figures using a uniform drift assumption. Actual costs depend on blower size, number of sensors, DO setpoints, and site-specific fouling rates. The direction is consistent: intervals that let drift accumulate past your control tolerance cost more than the calibration events they deferred.

What the historian also shows

When you pull the calibration records from the historian, you are likely to see a second pattern: step changes in sensor output immediately after calibration. Some of these reflect real pre-calibration drift being corrected. Others reflect calibration error: a sensor re-zeroed with a small bubble on the membrane, or calibrated in a bucket of tap water at a different temperature than the basin. Frequent calibration events introduce more opportunities for calibration error, particularly in plants with high technician turnover.

The right interval is one that keeps drift within your control tolerance while keeping calibration frequency low enough that each calibration event can be done carefully. For most activated sludge applications with polarographic sensors, that is typically in the two-to-three-week range when fouling is measured and the drift curve is actually checked, not simply assumed to match the manufacturer default.

The underlying condition

Whether the calibration schedule is two weeks or six, the aeration control loop operates on sensor output, not on the actual dissolved oxygen concentration. When the interval is appropriate and calibrations are executed correctly, the gap between what the sensor says and what the process holds is small. When the interval is too long, or when calibrations are missed due to staffing constraints or maintenance backlog, the control loop can drift significantly from its design intent.

The analysis that reveals this is in the historian. The drift records are already there: pre-calibration versus post-calibration readings, blower runtimes, DO trends. The pattern of drift accumulation and its effect on blower behavior is visible at cycle resolution, which typically means five-minute data over a 30-to-90-day window.

This is the same kind of pattern identified in the parallel-basin drift analysis and expanded in what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant. The cooling tower equivalent -- conductivity sensor drift triggering premature blowdown -- is documented in cooling tower blowdown control: conductivity drift cost. The DO calibration interval problem is not a different issue; it is the same measurement gap operating on a longer time scale.

If you want to understand whether your DO calibration intervals are matched to your actual process fouling rates, the starting point is the calibration and historian data you already have. item.title: Cooling tower blowdown control: conductivity drift cost
item.description: Conductivity sensor drift triggers premature blowdown, wasting makeup water and chemicals. Here is what it costs and how to detect it in your data.
item.content:encoded:
Conductivity blowdown control works by measuring dissolved solids in the cooling tower basin continuously and comparing that reading to a programmed setpoint. When conductivity crosses the setpoint -- chosen to match the system's design cycles of concentration (COC) -- a controller opens the blowdown valve, discharging concentrated basin water and replacing it with fresh makeup. COC is the ratio of dissolved solids in circulating water to incoming makeup: at six cycles, the system extracts six passes of evaporative cooling from each gallon before discharging. The DOE Federal Energy Management Program documents a 50 percent reduction in blowdown volume when moving from three to six COC. The conductivity sensor controls that entire difference. When that sensor has an offset, the system runs at the wrong COC regardless of what the control display shows.

Conductivity sensor drift in cooling tower blowdown control costs money in two directions. A sensor reading high triggers blowdown when basin water is still within its design operating range, discharging water that had remaining evaporative capacity. A sensor reading low allows dissolved solids to concentrate past the setpoint, depositing scale on heat transfer surfaces and potentially pushing discharge chemistry past permit limits. The DOE Federal Energy Management Program documents a 50 percent reduction in blowdown when moving from three to six cycles of concentration: the conductivity measurement controls that entire difference. When the sensor has an offset, the system is not running at the cycles the treatment program was designed for, regardless of what the control display shows. The detection method is below. The data is already in the historian.

How conductivity blowdown control works

A conductivity sensor in the basin or blowdown line reads dissolved solids continuously. A controller compares that reading to a programmed setpoint corresponding to the design cycles of concentration (COC). When the reading crosses the setpoint, the blowdown valve opens and fresh makeup water replaces what was discharged. The system is designed to run at the highest COC the water chemistry can sustain, since higher COC means less water discarded per unit of cooling output. The DOE Federal Energy Management Program documents a 20 percent reduction in makeup water and a 50 percent reduction in blowdown when moving from 3 to 6 COC -- a difference controlled entirely by where the sensor's reading lands relative to actual basin concentration. (DOE FEMP Best Management Practice #10: Cooling Tower Management)

How to detect conductivity sensor drift before it accumulates cost:

  1. Cross-check with a calibrated handheld meter at each maintenance visit. A divergence of more than 5 percent means the loop measurement should not be trusted to control blowdown until recalibrated.
  2. Pull blowdown valve timestamps and conductivity readings from the historian for a rolling 60-day window. Rising event frequency with stable makeup water quality points to the sensor, not the process.
  3. Track blowdown events normalized to cooling load. Fouling-driven high-bias drift appears as more blowdown events per unit of heat rejection over time, with no change in ambient conditions or system load to explain it.
  4. Compare makeup water conductivity readings over the same period. If makeup quality is stable and blowdown frequency is rising, the sensor or the controller setpoint has changed -- not the incoming water.

Why cycles of concentration are the performance metric

The conductivity setpoint corresponds directly to cycles of concentration: the ratio of dissolved solids in the circulating water compared to the makeup water. At three cycles of concentration, the circulating water is three times as concentrated as the incoming makeup. At six cycles, it is six times as concentrated, meaning the system has extracted six times the evaporative cooling work from each unit of water before discharging it.

The Department of Energy's Federal Energy Management Program, in its Best Management Practice for Cooling Tower Management, documents the consequence of that difference: increasing cycles from three to six reduces cooling tower makeup water consumption by 20 percent and cooling tower blowdown by 50 percent. (DOE FEMP Best Management Practice #10: Cooling Tower Management)

Most cooling towers run at two to four cycles of concentration. The practical ceiling is set by water chemistry: calcium, magnesium, silica, and other dissolved minerals will eventually scale heat exchange surfaces or corrode metal components if concentration runs too high. Water treatment programs add scale inhibitors and corrosion inhibitors specifically to allow higher cycles of concentration without those chemistry problems. But there is a second constraint that receives less attention: the accuracy of the conductivity measurement that tells the system what concentration it is actually running at.

What sensor drift does to blowdown frequency

Conductivity sensors in cooling tower service face a corrosive environment. Basin water contains biological growth, suspended solids, scale-forming minerals, and treatment chemicals. Sensor fouling from biofilm and mineral deposits is the most common failure mode, and the most common direction of failure is a reading that drifts high: a deposit on the sensor surface creates an impedance that the controller interprets as elevated dissolved solids in the water.

A sensor reading high produces the same control response as actual high concentration: it triggers blowdown. If the setpoint is 1,500 microsiemens per centimeter and the sensor reads 1,600 when the actual basin conductivity is 1,200, the controller sees an out-of-spec condition and opens the valve. The water being discharged was at 1,200 microsiemens, well within the setpoint, and capable of running through additional evaporative cycles before requiring blowdown.

This is not a hypothetical edge case. Sensor fouling accumulates gradually, and in many plants the cleaning interval for conductivity sensors is set by a calendar schedule rather than by measurement-to-measurement agreement. A sensor cleaned monthly in a high-load summer period is operating for weeks with accumulating offset. During that interval, every blowdown event the offset triggers is water the system did not need to discharge.

The reverse failure also occurs: a sensor that reads low because of a calibration shift or a failed element delays blowdown past the intended setpoint. Scale begins depositing on heat transfer surfaces, thermal performance drops, and in severe cases chemical treatment effectiveness falls as the system runs beyond its design envelope. Scale deposits of even 1/16 inch on heat exchanger surfaces can reduce thermal efficiency by roughly 10 percent. (Rahmani et al., Applied Thermal Engineering, 2017, doi:10.1016/j.applthermaleng.2016.10.191)

Quantifying the cost of over-blowdown

The DOE documents a 50 percent reduction in blowdown when moving from three to six cycles of concentration, and that figure provides a basis for estimating what premature blowdown costs. The calculation depends on facility size, local water costs, and sewer discharge fees, but the structure is consistent:

At a facility with 1 million gallons per day of makeup water:

Operating scenarioApproximate daily makeup waterApproximate daily blowdown
6 cycles of concentration (design intent)1,000,000 gallons~200,000 gallons
3 cycles of concentration (sensor reads high)1,200,000+ gallons~400,000 gallons
Difference from premature blowdown200,000+ gallons/day~200,000 gallons/day

Modelled example using DOE FEMP documented percentage differences; actual values depend on evaporation rate, local water chemistry, and the degree of sensor offset.

That makeup water difference carries three layers of cost. First, water purchase cost: industrial water rates vary by region, but an industrial facility paying in the range of $1 to $5 per thousand gallons for purchased water faces a material cost when hundreds of thousands of gallons per day are discharged unnecessarily. Second, sewer and wastewater discharge costs: many jurisdictions charge for cooling tower blowdown discharge separately from water purchase, and in areas with sewer surcharges for high-conductivity industrial discharge, this cost can approach or exceed the water purchase cost. Third, chemical treatment cost: every gallon of blowdown replaced with fresh makeup water requires treatment chemicals to protect the system from the new makeup water's chemistry.

For facilities that discharge cooling tower blowdown directly to surface waters, there is a fourth cost layer: regulatory exposure. Cooling tower blowdown discharged to waters of the United States requires authorization under the EPA's National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System (NPDES) program, and industrial discharge permits for many categories include limits on specific conductance or total dissolved solids as a proxy for concentrated minerals and treatment chemicals. A sensor reading low (allowing cycles of concentration to run above design) may produce a discharge that exceeds permit limits even when the control system appears to be operating normally, because the system registers a conductivity that is within setpoint while actual basin concentration has climbed past it. (40 CFR Part 122, EPA NPDES Permit Regulations)

None of this is visible at the level of a single blowdown event. It becomes visible in trends: makeup water consumption trending upward over a season, chemical feed rates increasing without a corresponding change in makeup water quality, blowdown frequency in the historian rising faster than ambient temperature or load would predict.

The diagnostic that is already in the historian

The same diagnostic approach that reveals DO sensor drift in aeration systems applies to conductivity sensor drift in cooling tower control. The data is in the historian: blowdown valve timestamps, conductivity sensor readings, makeup water flow, and any makeup water quality monitoring already being logged.

The signature of a sensor reading high is blowdown events that cluster at a conductivity reading just above the setpoint, while makeup water conductivity readings stay constant and blowdown event frequency increases over time on a consistent load. The signature of a sensor reading low is the opposite: infrequent blowdown with conductivity readings that stay below the setpoint even as the tower accumulates load, followed eventually by scale chemistry indicators or pressure-drop increases in the heat exchangers.

This is a temporal version of the spatial drift problem described in a parallel-equipment analysis. In that case, two identical aeration basins showed diverging blower runtime and energy use that reflected sensor offset rather than actual process differences. Here, the same principle operates over time in a single system: the measurement feeding the control loop has an offset, the loop acts on the offset rather than the process state, and the cost accumulates in the historian before it appears anywhere else.

The full parallel-basin methodology is in why parallel equipment drifts apart, and what the gap costs. For data centers where cooling tower blowdown directly affects the WUE metric, the connection between sensor drift and reported efficiency is covered in data center WUE: what the metric measures, what it misses, and what it takes to move it.

What accurate conductivity measurement enables

When the conductivity sensor controlling blowdown is reading accurately and corrected between calibration intervals, the control system can run the tower at the cycles of concentration the water treatment program was designed for. The 20 to 50 percent water savings the DOE documents from moving from three to six cycles are achievable without chemistry changes or capital investment -- they require that the measurement driving the control loop reflects actual basin conditions.

For industrial facilities with large cooling loads -- power generation, petrochemical, food and beverage processing, large manufacturing plants -- the difference between running at three cycles and six cycles is not a marginal optimization. At the scale of a 2,000-ton cooling tower system, it is a question of hundreds of thousands of gallons per day.

The diagnostic questions are straightforward. Is the conductivity sensor reading the same at the start and end of a calibration interval? Does blowdown frequency track makeup water conductivity the way it should, or does it drift independently? Are blowdown events triggering at the expected conductivity setpoint, or consistently below it? The answers are in the historian. The constraint is having a way to pull the data at the resolution that shows blowdown-event-level behavior over a long enough window to separate sensor drift from process variation.

If your cooling tower water use has trended upward or your blowdown frequency looks inconsistent with your system load, the control data is already in your historian.

item.title: In Water Online: the $1.5 million sewer repair and the water-quality evidence missing upstream
item.description: Our guest column in Water Online on what a $1.5 million sewer restitution case shows about the gap between measuring a discharge and explaining what caused it upstream.
item.content:encoded:
Water Online published a guest column by Alex Towfigh, AquaMesh's founder and CEO, on 26 October 2026. The full piece is on the Water Online site: The $1.5 Million Sewer Repair — And The Water-Quality Evidence Missing Upstream.

What follows is a short summary.

The argument in brief

The case. A California wire manufacturer was ordered to pay $1.5 million in restitution after acidic wastewater damaged a public trunk sewer. EPA's 2010 announcement described 14 illegal discharges over four months of 2008, with pH as low as 1 against a permit minimum of 6. The column is careful about what this shows: the restitution covered cumulative damage, and a new analyzer alone would not necessarily have stopped the discharges. Its question is whether the plant could have recognized a repeated pattern early enough to investigate the treatment system behind it.

An endpoint is not an explanation. A pH probe at the discharge point tells you whether neutralization worked. It does not tell you whether the cause was a transfer, a dosing fault, a bypass, a reagent shortage or maintenance. Better detection cannot replace working treatment equipment, but it can shorten the path from a suspect reading to its cause.

Two bills for the same discharge. Lost product and treatment surcharges are separate ledgers, and the column warns against counting the same saving twice. It works through a dairy scenario using a published loss range of 1% to 3% of milk processed, and a COD example using San Diego's published January 2026 rate of $0.27 per pound: at 1 million gallons a day with 1,000 mg/L of added COD, about $2,252 a day. Both are sensitivity calculations, not measured losses or billing forecasts, and the column says so.

The blind spot between systems. Read-only access to PLC, SCADA and historian data reconstructs what production was doing and when. A multiwavelength UV/visible sensor can show changes in the stream that pH, flow or conductivity miss, provided it is calibrated on site. A rinse that lines up with an optical change is a lead to check against a lab sample, not a finding.

The clock decides usefulness. Detection only helps if it arrives in time to act. EPA event-detection research found that many unexpected water-quality changes came from operational changes or sensor problems rather than contamination. So the measures that matter are lead time, confirmed causes, false alerts per shift and cost, not anomaly accuracy on its own.

Three questions for the next operations meeting

For each recurring discharge, the column asks:

  1. What is the earliest validated water-quality measurement?
  2. Which upstream records would explain it?
  3. What authorized operating change would prevent it from happening again?

It closes with a test of its own: find the single missing measurement that would most improve the conclusion. If there isn't one, more sensors may not be the right investment. And AquaMesh's value has to be shown the same way, through lower confirmed losses, earlier diagnosis or less investigation effort.

Read the full column in Water Online.

item.title: Intermittent aeration: why DO sensor precision matters
item.description: DO sensor precision controls whether intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal saves energy or misses permit limits. Here is what happens when it drifts.
item.content:encoded:
Biological nitrogen removal is one of the more demanding process control challenges in activated sludge treatment. Plants with tight effluent nitrogen limits need to run two competing biological processes: nitrification under aerobic conditions and denitrification under anoxic ones, efficiently, in the same biological system. For plants using intermittent aeration to accomplish this in a single-basin configuration, the precision of dissolved oxygen control during aeration cycles is not an instrumentation detail. It is the variable that determines whether the strategy works.

What intermittent aeration is trying to do

Conventional biological nitrogen removal stages aerobic and anoxic zones in sequence: ammonia is nitrified to nitrate in an aerated zone, then denitrified to nitrogen gas in a downstream anoxic zone. The system is reliable but capital-intensive and requires careful hydraulic design.

Intermittent aeration takes a different path: the same basin alternates between aerobic and anoxic phases by cycling blowers on and off. During the aerated phase, nitrifiers convert ammonia to nitrate. During the unaerated phase, denitrifiers reduce nitrate to nitrogen gas, using carbon already present in the mixed liquor. Some organisms can carry out both reactions near-simultaneously at low dissolved oxygen concentrations, a phenomenon called simultaneous nitrification-denitrification (SND). The EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual identifies low-DO operation, typically below 1.0 mg/L, as a condition that promotes SND in conventional activated sludge by creating anoxic microsites within biological flocs. (EPA, Nutrient Control Design Manual, 2010, Section 5)

A 2022 review in Chemical Engineering Journal analyzed over 50 intermittent aeration studies and found that precise DO control during aeration phases was the most consistent predictor of nitrogen removal efficiency, ahead of cycle length or influent carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. (Miao et al., 2022, Chemical Engineering Journal, doi:10.1016/j.cej.2021.133516)

The practical appeal is real: intermittent aeration can achieve substantial nitrogen removal without a separate anoxic zone, with lower aeration energy than continuous-aeration systems, and with flexible response to variable influent loads. These advantages depend on cycle timing, and cycle timing depends on DO measurement.

Where DO control precision comes in

The cycle timing in intermittent aeration is almost always governed by a dissolved oxygen setpoint rather than a fixed timer. Aeration turns on when DO falls below a lower bound; it turns off when DO rises above an upper bound. The accuracy of that DO band controls the effectiveness of the strategy:

Sensor reading low (common fouling failure): A sensor that reads 0.4 mg/L when actual DO is 1.8 mg/L keeps blowers running long past the point where nitrification has completed. The aerobic phase extends beyond the design intent. The anoxic fraction shrinks. Denitrification suffers, nitrogen removal drops, and the plant uses more electricity than the intermittent strategy was supposed to require.

Sensor reading high: Aeration shuts off early. The basin does not complete nitrification in one cycle. Ammonia carries over. In a plant with a permit nitrogen limit, this is an effluent compliance risk, not just an energy problem.

Fouling that accumulates between cycles: Mixed liquor accumulates on membrane or optical sensor surfaces during the unaerated phase. When aeration restarts, the sensor enters the aerobic phase with an offset that compounds over successive cycles if cleaning intervals are not calibrated to match actual fouling rates. What those intervals should be for activated sludge service is covered in DO sensor calibration intervals in activated sludge.

The cumulative effect is that the DO setpoints operators specify on the control screen may not correspond to the dissolved oxygen concentration the organisms experience. The blower control loop optimizes against a sensor output, not against the process state.

What this looks like in practice

The same phenomenon described in the parallel-basin aeration analysis applies here in a temporal rather than spatial dimension. In that case, two basins running simultaneously showed a DO divergence that reflected sensor drift rather than process differences: one blower was pinned at maximum output, consuming over $3,000 per year more than its twin, for the full 25-day record. The spatial version was visible by comparing basins side by side. The parallel equipment drift analysis is in why parallel equipment drifts apart, and the full historian data methodology is in what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant.

The temporal version in intermittent aeration requires a different analysis: charting DO sensor output against blower on/off timestamps at five-minute or finer resolution, and comparing aerobic phase duration over time. A sensor reading accurately produces aerobic phases of consistent duration for a given influent load. A sensor that is drifting produces phases that systematically lengthen (reading low, blowers run long) or shorten (reading high, blowers cut off early) in ways that do not track influent load changes.

Both versions share the same root cause: the measurement feeding the control loop has an offset that the loop cannot self-detect, because there is no independent reference running alongside it.

The energy calculation for intermittent aeration

The aeration energy baseline for secondary treatment, around 1,500 kWh per million gallons for activated sludge, assumes reasonably continuous aeration. Intermittent aeration in a nitrogen-removal configuration typically aims to reduce aeration runtime to 50 to 70 percent of total time, depending on the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the influent and the cycle design. That would imply aeration energy in the range of 750 to 1,050 kWh per million gallons when timing is accurate.

At a 10 MGD plant and the current EIA industrial rate of $0.0977 per kWh (EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026), the difference between accurate intermittent aeration (approximately 900 kWh/MG as a midpoint) and sensor-extended aeration (1,500 kWh/MG because the sensor is holding blowers on too long) is approximately $215,000 per year at that scale.

Modelled example for a 10 MGD plant with intermittent aeration:

Accurate DO controlDO sensor drifting low
Aeration runtime share60%100% (effectively continuous)
Estimated kWh/MG9001,500
Annual energy cost at $0.098/kWh$193,100$321,900
Annual cost difference$128,800

This is a modelled example using published benchmarks; actual values depend on plant-specific loading, cycle design, and the degree of sensor offset. The direction is consistent: sensor drift in an intermittent aeration system does not only affect nitrogen removal performance. It erodes the energy savings that justified the intermittent strategy in the first place.

What accurate DO measurement enables

When DO measurement in an intermittent aeration system is continuous, accurate, and corrected against drift between calibration intervals, the control loop can do what it was designed for: maintain the aerobic-to-anoxic balance that both nitrification and denitrification require.

For plants approaching permit limits on total nitrogen, the margin for process error is narrow. A sensor that introduces a systematic offset into the timing of aeration cycles is a measurement problem that manifests as an effluent compliance risk. The issue is usually visible in the historian data before it appears in the permit reporting: aerobic phase durations extending over time, DO baseline at cycle start gradually increasing, nitrogen removal efficiency declining in ways that do not correlate with influent load.

The diagnostic questions are the same ones that apply to continuous aeration systems. Are the DO sensors reading accurately between calibrations? Does blower runtime at a given influent load match what the setpoints predict? Are cycle times stable, or are they drifting? The methodology for that analysis is in aeration energy at wastewater plants: the cost, the waste, and the measurement gap.

None of this analysis requires new hardware. The data is in the historian. The constraint is having a way to extract it at the resolution that shows cycle-level behavior, over a long enough window, against a reference that was not subject to the same drift.

If your plant uses intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal and you want to understand whether your DO control is performing as designed, the place to start is the cycle data already in your historian.

item.title: Data center WUE: what it measures and what it misses
item.description: WUE measures liters per kWh of IT load. It does not show where water goes, verify cooling controls, or prove tower savings for reporting.
item.content:encoded:
Water Usage Effectiveness (WUE) is a data center water metric introduced by The Green Grid. The formula: liters of water consumed at the facility divided by kilowatt-hours delivered to IT equipment, where lower is better and zero is the theoretical ideal.

What WUE does not answer:

  • Where the water is going (evaporation versus blowdown)
  • Whether the sensors driving cooling tower control are accurate
  • Whether blowdown volume can be reduced on demand under reporting or drought rules
  • What specific operating changes move the number versus what is fixed by physics

Each of those gaps affects whether a WUE target in a sustainability report is operationally achievable.

What WUE actually measures

The metric was introduced by The Green Grid as a companion to PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Like PUE, it is a ratio: lower is better and zero is the theoretical ideal. A site with a WUE of 2.0 consumes two liters of water for every kilowatt-hour its servers use.

Research on actual facility performance puts the range between 1 and 9 liters per kilowatt-hour depending on cooling approach, climate zone, and facility age, with a central tendency around 1.5 to 2 L/kWh for older evaporative cooling installations. (Mytton, D. "Data centre water consumption." npj Clean Water 4, 52 (2021)) Newer hyperscale builds using advanced chemistry management or closed-loop cooling report considerably lower values.

WUE is typically calculated annually. Some operators report quarterly. It is a useful benchmark for comparing facilities against each other and tracking long-run progress. It is a poor guide for what to do on Tuesday.

Where the water actually goes

For facilities using evaporative cooling towers, which covers the majority of installed capacity, the water balance has two main terms: evaporation and blowdown.

Evaporation is the productive part. The cooling process works by letting water absorb heat and leave the tower as vapor. Roughly 70 to 80 percent of the water that enters the tower in this way is not recoverable; it has done its job and left the site. (Mytton 2021) This fraction tracks the heat load on the facility and varies with ambient wet-bulb temperature. A site cannot significantly reduce evaporative losses without changing the physics of how it cools its equipment.

Blowdown is different. As water circulates through the tower and a portion evaporates, the dissolved minerals left behind concentrate. Calcium, silica, chlorides, and biological material accumulate. If concentration rises too high, scale deposits on heat exchanger surfaces and corrosion accelerates. To prevent this, some fraction of the circulating water is periodically discharged and replaced with fresh makeup water. That discharge is blowdown.

The ratio of dissolved mineral concentration in the circulating water to the concentration in the makeup supply is called the cycles of concentration. At three cycles, for every gallon that evaporates, roughly half a gallon is discharged as blowdown, and one and a half gallons are drawn in as makeup. At six cycles, blowdown drops to roughly one fifth of the evaporation volume. At ten cycles, it drops to one ninth.

Modelled example: For a 10-megawatt IT load facility with a moderate WUE of 2.0 L/kWh operating at 85 percent utilization, annual water consumption is roughly 149 million liters. If evaporation represents 75 percent of that total, the remaining 37 million liters per year is blowdown. Moving from 3 to 6 cycles of concentration reduces that blowdown component by approximately 60 percent, or 22 million liters per year. This is a modelled estimate based on the ratios above; actual results depend on makeup water chemistry, heat load profile, and seasonal variation.

The measurement problem

The control system that manages blowdown uses a conductivity sensor as its primary input. Conductivity in the circulating water rises as dissolved minerals concentrate, and the controller uses this as a proxy for cycles of concentration. When conductivity reaches a set threshold, the blowdown valve opens and makeup water flows in.

This means the conductivity sensor, sitting in a basin or on a sidestream line, is the direct operational driver of water efficiency performance. A sensor that reads accurately and holds its calibration enables tight control at higher cycles. A sensor that has fouled, drifted, or been calibrated infrequently has the opposite effect.

A sensor reading low when concentration is actually high causes the controller to keep the blowdown valve closed longer than intended. Dissolved solids accumulate beyond design limits. Scale risk increases and the operator may not know it until a heat exchanger inspection. A sensor reading high when concentration is actually normal causes the controller to open the blowdown valve prematurely and repeatedly, discharging good water and drawing in fresh makeup water unnecessarily. The facility's WUE is higher than it needs to be, and the cause does not appear in the annual report.

Neither failure mode triggers an alarm in a standard building management system. The control loop is running. The conductivity reading is within the operating range. The controller is doing exactly what it was programmed to do with the signal it receives.

This is the same silent failure pattern that affects dissolved oxygen control in wastewater aeration basins, where a fouled sensor drives blowers toward wasted energy rather than toward needed oxygen. The structure of the problem is identical: a lagging indicator (WUE for water, energy per gallon treated for wastewater) does not point to the sensor drift that is the actual cause. The gap shows up only when you look at the control inputs directly, not at the outcomes they produce. The parallel is covered in more detail in the analysis of why parallel equipment drifts apart. It also applies to intermittent aeration cycles for nitrogen removal, where DO sensor drift affects both effluent compliance and the energy savings the intermittent strategy was meant to deliver: intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal: what DO sensor precision actually controls.

For a detailed breakdown of what conductivity sensor drift costs in cooling tower water volume and chemical spend, including a worked example using DOE benchmark data, see cooling tower blowdown control: what conductivity sensor drift costs in water and chemicals.

Proving cooling tower water savings for reporting

A WUE target in a sustainability disclosure or a California Water Scarcity Plan is defensible only if three things are in place: a metered baseline, an auditable record of the variables that drive consumption, and a method to demonstrate the change was real rather than a calculation artifact.

For cooling towers, that means measuring at the points where water actually enters and leaves the system.

Metering checklist

  • Makeup water flow: A flow meter on the makeup supply line, totalizing by day. This is the primary input: it is what the utility invoices and what regulators count as consumption. Without a direct makeup meter, total consumption is estimated from conductivity readings and design assumptions, and that estimate cannot catch sensor-driven overconsumption.
  • Blowdown volume: A flow meter or timed valve record on the blowdown line. Blowdown is the discretionary water loss, the portion a facility can actually reduce through chemistry management. Without a direct measurement, blowdown is typically back-calculated from conductivity set points, which creates circular logic if the conductivity sensor is the variable under audit.
  • Basin conductivity with historian logging: A continuous conductivity reading linked to the historian, not just a set-point indicator. The logged record shows what cycles of concentration the facility actually operated at over time, versus what the design target was. This is the evidence base for any claim that COC improved.
  • Conductivity sensor verification schedule: A periodic grab-sample check using an independent meter compared against the installed sensor. The DOE Federal Energy Management Program Best Management Practice 10 identifies conductivity monitoring and cycles-of-concentration tracking as core elements of water efficiency for cooling towers. A documented record of sensor verification during both the baseline and the improvement period is the evidence that the signal driving blowdown control was accurate.

Establishing an auditable baseline

A baseline for a WUE improvement claim needs at least 12 months of data before the change, covering seasonal variation in wet-bulb temperature and heat load. Cooling water consumption tracks ambient conditions, and a baseline drawn only from summer months overstates annual average performance.

From that record, calculate:

  1. Average cycles of concentration by month
  2. Makeup volume relative to evaporative load (calculable from heat load data and ambient conditions)
  3. Blowdown as a percentage of total makeup, by month
  4. Unexplained blowdown events: volume spikes not correlated with changes in heat load

Unexplained events, whether from conductivity sensor drift, a valve held open during maintenance, or a chemical feed miscalculation, show up as isolated increases in blowdown volume not matched by heat load increases. In a 25-day historian review at an industrial process facility, three anomalies of this type were identified, adding an estimated 12 to 18 percent to water consumption for that period. (What a 25-day historian audit finds at a treatment plant) The same review methodology applies directly to cooling tower makeup and blowdown logs.

When direct blowdown metering is not installed

Many operating data centers lack a flow meter on the blowdown line. Blowdown volume is inferred from the conductivity set point and the makeup meter, which means the calculated efficiency number cannot detect the cases where the sensor controlling blowdown is drifting. A dedicated blowdown meter converts an estimated variable into a verified one. For a site preparing a California Water Scarcity Plan, that difference is material: a commitment to reduce blowdown by a specific percentage is auditable only if blowdown is measured independently of the control signal.

The California compliance context

California's AB 2619, signed in September 2026, requires data center operators to report total and direct annual water use by source at every business license renewal, under penalty of perjury. AB 2469 requires a Water Scarcity Plan by 2028 for facilities requiring construction permits. (California data center water reporting requirements)

A Water Scarcity Plan is a commitment to reduce water consumption under specified drought conditions, including staged curtailment and targeted reductions by use type. The commitment is credible only if the site can demonstrate that it knows where its water goes and can reduce specific uses on demand.

A site operating at three cycles of concentration because its conductivity sensors drift between maintenance intervals cannot reliably commit to operating at six cycles under drought conditions. The chemistry that makes six cycles safe to operate requires measurement quality that makes four and a half cycles the actual operational average. The gap between the plan and the operational reality is a sensor reliability problem, not a strategy problem.

Three questions worth checking before setting a WUE target

Before writing a WUE improvement target into a sustainability report or a Water Scarcity Plan, three questions are worth answering from existing historian data.

What are your actual cycles of concentration, by tower? This is calculable from makeup flow, blowdown flow, and conductivity readings. If the number is consistently below design, the control logic or the sensor driving it is worth examining before adjusting targets.

How does blowdown volume correlate with wet-bulb temperature? Evaporation tracks ambient conditions predictably. Blowdown should not spike independently of heat load. Unexplained blowdown events in the historian are almost always sensor artifacts or valve events, not chemistry responses.

What share of total water use does blowdown represent? If blowdown is running above 30 percent of total consumption on a facility that should be operating at moderate cycles, the conductivity control system is not performing at design. This shows up in 12 months of metered data and does not require a new study to identify.

None of this analysis requires capital investment. The data exists in most historian systems. The constraint is usually having a way to look at it with enough resolution and the right reference points to distinguish signal from noise.

If your site is preparing for California's 2027 renewal requirements or developing a scarcity plan for 2028, the water balance question is worth addressing before the commitment is made, not after. item.title: Wastewater aeration energy: cost and the measurement gap
item.description: Aeration is 50 to 75 percent of a wastewater plant's electricity bill. What it costs per MGD, why the savings erode, and how to cut blower energy without new equipment.
item.content:encoded:
Aeration is the single largest line on the electricity bill for most activated sludge wastewater plants. Aeration systems typically represent 50 to 75 percent of total electricity consumption at activated sludge facilities. The logical response is to install dissolved oxygen sensors, add variable frequency drives to blowers, and let a control loop do the rest. Many plants have done exactly that. Not all of them kept the savings.

Here is what the cost actually looks like, why the standard fix often falls short, and how to recover blower energy without adding hardware.

How large the prize is

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported the national average industrial electricity rate at $0.0977 per kWh in July 2026, up from $0.0933 the prior year. (EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026)

Secondary treatment activated sludge plants typically use between 1,200 and 1,800 kWh per million gallons treated. The EPA's water and wastewater energy management documentation cites a common benchmark near 1,500 kWh per million gallons for secondary treatment. (U.S. EPA, Ensuring a Sustainable Future: An Energy Management Guidebook for Wastewater and Water Utilities)

Modelled example for a 10 MGD secondary treatment plant:

Annual flow treated3,650 million gallons
Electricity at 1,500 kWh/MG5,475,000 kWh
Aeration share at 60%3,285,000 kWh
At $0.098/kWh industrial rate$321,900/year

This is a modelled example based on published benchmarks. Actual costs vary with load patterns, treatment configuration, equipment age, and the utility tariff in effect. The kilowatt-hours are the right order of magnitude; the dollar figure resolves once you pull an actual utility bill.

At this scale, a 20 percent reduction in blower energy is worth roughly $64,000 per year. The Florida Water and Pollution Control Operators Association published analysis in April 2026 showing that basic demand-based DO control typically reduces blower energy by 10 to 25 percent, and that PLC-optimized control can reach 20 to 40 percent. (FWPCOA, "Demand-Based DO Control And Energy Optimization," April 2026)

Those are compelling numbers. The problem is that they describe what the system saves when it is working as designed. The gap between the theoretical savings and what a plant actually captures and keeps is usually a measurement problem.

Where the savings go

A DO control loop has three components: a sensor reporting the current dissolved oxygen level, a controller comparing that reading to a setpoint, and a variable frequency drive adjusting blower output. The logic is straightforward.

The sensor is the weak link.

Electrochemical membranes foul and require regular replacement. Optical sensors are more stable but still accumulate biofilm in mixed liquor. A sensor that reads 1.8 mg/L when the actual basin concentration is 3.2 mg/L signals the controller that the basin is under-oxygenated. The controller responds by running blowers harder. The plant pays for electricity that achieves nothing useful, and nothing in the system indicates anything is wrong.

The inverse failure is less common but more consequential: a sensor fouled in a way that reads artificially high causes the controller to back off blowers when DO is genuinely borderline, with the process instability that follows.

Both failure modes are silent. The control loop is running. No alarms fire. The historian records the sensor output without knowing it has drifted. Operators checking the dashboard see normal-looking DO values.

This is why many plants install DO control hardware and see strong early results followed by gradual erosion. The hardware is still there. The control loop is still active. But the measurement feeding it has drifted, and the loop is now optimizing against a wrong input.

The parallel basin case

Plants with multiple aeration basins running in parallel face a compounding version of this problem. Sensors in different basins drift at different rates depending on local solids loading, position relative to diffusers, and how consistently each one gets cleaned. The basins may share a common air header, but if their DO sensors are reading different offsets, the blower outputs serving them will diverge in ways that reflect sensor drift rather than actual process differences.

We covered the mechanics and cost of this kind of hidden divergence in why parallel equipment drifts apart. The direct energy cost of an over-aerated basin shows up in blower runtime. The downstream cost in nitrogen removal performance, when an anoxic zone receives excess dissolved oxygen, is harder to price but real.

What the historian data showed

When we analyzed 25 days of historian data from an operating plant earlier this year, one of the first findings was a DO-driven blower anomaly: one basin was running at more than three times the DO level of its parallel twin, with its blower pinned at maximum output, for the full duration of the record.

Both basins drew on the same shared air header. The control loop was functioning. The deviation was visible only by comparing the two basins side by side at hourly resolution. A daily manual grab from either basin, taken at a representative time, could easily have missed it.

The finding was worth $3,316 per year in direct blower power, plus the process risk from carrying excess oxygen into a downstream anoxic zone. It was already in the data. It just had not been looked at in this way. The full analysis is in what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant.

What accurate measurement changes

When DO measurement is continuous, accurate, and does not accumulate drift between calibration cycles, the control loop has what it was designed to work from. Blower output tracks actual oxygen demand rather than sensor artifacts. Setpoints can be tightened because operators are not building in a buffer to account for measurement uncertainty.

For plants running intermittent aeration for simultaneous nitrification/denitrification, the DO swing required is fast and narrow. The economics of that strategy depend entirely on measurement that responds quickly and without offset.

Some plants extend this further with online analyzers for ammonium or nitrate to feed an ammonia-based aeration control loop. Those instruments use a different measurement principle than a DO probe, and what they actually detect versus what they are marketed as measuring matters before you specify one. Spectral change analysis versus calibrated parameters covers the distinction.

Accurate measurement also creates a defensible record of what happened. When a plant documents savings for a utility incentive program or a regulatory report, both the baseline and current performance need measurement that holds up to scrutiny.

The same measurement-loop dynamic drives water waste in cooling towers, where a conductivity sensor reading high causes the system to discharge water still within operating range. The cost structure for that failure mode is in cooling tower blowdown control: what conductivity sensor drift costs in water and chemicals.

How to cut blower energy without new equipment

The FWPCOA analysis cited above documents 10 to 40 percent reductions in blower energy from demand-based DO control, compared to running blowers without feedback. Plants already running VFDs in manual mode, or with feedback loops that have not been recommissioned since original installation, often have most of that gap still available. The five steps below work in sequence; later steps depend on the earlier ones being in place.

1. Verify DO sensor accuracy before adjusting any setpoint. A setpoint change based on a drifted sensor moves the control loop to a different wrong reference. The first step is confirming what the sensor is actually reading, using a calibrated portable meter at different times of day and across the full diurnal load range, not just immediately after cleaning or calibration. This establishes whether subsequent steps are starting from an accurate baseline. How often DO sensors should be recalibrated in activated sludge mixed liquor, and what calibration intervals are appropriate for different sensor types, is covered in DO sensor calibration intervals in activated sludge.

2. Reduce the DO setpoint to the process minimum your permit allows. Most activated sludge systems designed for BOD removal can sustain full nitrification at setpoints between 1.5 and 2.0 mg/L. The EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual (2010, Section 5) documents that nitrification in suspended-growth systems can proceed at dissolved oxygen concentrations as low as 0.5 mg/L, with typical operating setpoints higher to buffer for load variation. If your plant is running a legacy setpoint of 2.5 or 3.0 mg/L without a process reason for it, the difference is directly recoverable blower energy. (EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual, 2010)

3. Close the feedback loop if it is running open. VFDs installed without an active PID loop holding them to a DO setpoint are often switched to manual by operators who found manual mode more predictable. An open-loop VFD captures some savings compared to a fixed-speed motor but none of the demand-following reduction that justifies the installation. Closing the loop requires that step 1 is true: the feedback signal has to be accurate, or the closed loop will chase measurement noise.

4. Set blower discharge pressure to the minimum the diffuser system requires. Discharge pressure setpoints are frequently established at commissioning and not revisited. Reducing header pressure in measured increments, while monitoring airflow distribution and DO response across the basin, identifies how much design margin was left in place. The installed blower manufacturer's pressure-power curve quantifies the energy difference for the specific unit; it should be in the plant files or is available from the manufacturer directly.

5. Stage blower capacity to follow actual oxygen demand. Running extra standby capacity continuously, or cycling blowers on a fixed time schedule regardless of load, keeps equipment running in inefficient operating regions. A staging sequence that adds or drops blower capacity based on measured demand keeps each running unit nearer its design point. For plants with multiple basins and a shared air header, the parallel-basin divergence problem can mask whether staging is working as intended; blower runtime comparisons across basins are a useful check.

None of these changes requires new equipment. Steps 2 through 5 all depend on step 1 being correct, because a setpoint, a feedback loop, a pressure target, or a staging sequence that starts from a drifted sensor reading optimizes against the wrong input.

Three questions worth asking before tuning the control loop

Before commissioning a new aeration control strategy or investigating why existing savings have eroded, three questions are worth answering directly from available data.

Are the DO sensors reading accurately? A comparison between sensor output and a calibrated handheld grab at different times of day, not just right after calibration, shows whether a sensor is holding its reading or drifting between service intervals.

What does the blower run-time history show? If blowers are running at sustained high output during periods when influent flow and temperature are moderate, the measurement feeding the control loop deserves examination before changing the control logic itself.

Are parallel basins loading evenly? Persistent divergence in blower output between basins handling equivalent loads is almost always a measurement issue. It rarely responds to setpoint adjustments alone.

None of these analyses requires new hardware. The data is usually in the historian. The constraint is having a way to look at it at the right resolution, over a long enough window, against the right reference.

If your plant is spending in the range described above, the measurement question is worth examining directly. An initial review of your historian data can show whether the control loop is working from accurate inputs and where the largest gaps are.
