item.title: In Dairy Foods: why dairy plants still miss their most expensive process losses
item.description: Our contributed article in Dairy Foods on where milk solids leave a plant unnoticed, why more historian tags alone cannot find them, and how to prove a saving one event at a time.
item.content:encoded:
Dairy Foods published a contributed article by Alex Towfigh, AquaMesh's founder and CEO, on 12 October 2026. The full piece is on the Dairy Foods site: Why dairy plants still miss their most expensive process losses.

What follows is a short summary. The article itself is exclusive to Dairy Foods.

The argument in brief

The losses happen during transitions. Published research puts routine losses of milk to sewer at 1% to 3% of the milk a plant processes. Most of it leaves during startups, interruptions, shutdowns and rinses: short windows where the pipe contents change and someone has to decide where product ends and water begins.

More tags do not fix a missing measurement. Conductivity tells you something changed, but not how much product is in the line. A flowmeter tells you how much is moving, but not what it is. Lab results come back after the decision has been made. If the plant never measured the chemistry, software running on the historian has nothing to analyze.

Spectral sensing helps, if it can be trusted. An optical spectrum carries far more information than a single-variable sensor. But temperature, bubbles, solids and a fouled window all move the reading. Without local calibration, a dirty window can look like a product loss, so every reading needs a confidence level attached.

Context decides what a signal means. Rising conductivity is expected during caustic circulation and alarming during a product transfer. The article describes starting from data the plant already has (CIP steps, valve positions, lab results) to establish operating state, adding sensing only where a real blind spot exists, and producing an explanation of what changed and why rather than another generic alarm.

Prove it one event at a time. Start read-only. Existing controls and sanitation checks stay in charge. Pick one expensive event, measure its baseline, catch it earlier, change the decision, and verify the result. One peer-reviewed UHT cleaning study cited in the piece used phase-endpoint measurement to cut a cleaning sequence from 142 to 66 minutes and roughly halve its effluent.

The article's dollar figures are sensitivity calculations at an illustrative plant scale, not measured results at any named facility. It says so, and so do we.

Read the full article in Dairy Foods.

item.title: California now asks data centers what they actually use, under penalty of perjury
item.description: Two bills signed on 21 September split a data center's water into total and direct use, by source, on every business license renewal. A third requirement lands in 2028. Most sites cannot currently answer either.
item.content:encoded:
On 21 September 2026 the Governor of California signed AB 2619, now Chapter 437 of the 2026 Statutes, and AB 2469 alongside it. Between them they change what a data center operator in California has to be able to say about water, and when.

The reporting obligation is the part worth reading closely, because it is more specific than the coverage suggests.

What AB 2619 actually asks for

AB 2619 works through the business license process rather than through a new permit. It sorts data centers into three types: Type I, or hyperscale, at more than 10,000 servers or more than 25 megawatts; Type II between 2 and 25 megawatts; and Type III below 2 megawatts.

At initial application, the operator gives the water supplier, and repeats on the license application form, a good faith estimate of expected water use, the anticipated source, and projected volume for the maximum day, the maximum month, and the average year.

At every renewal, the operator reports the preceding calendar year's annual water use (and here the statute is precise) "including total water use and direct water use," along with the cooling system type.

Direct annual water use is defined in the bill as:

The volume of water withdrawn, delivered, or otherwise used onsite for data center operations, including cooling, sanitation, irrigation, and any other operational use, identified by source, including potable water, nonpotable water, or recycled water.

All of it under penalty of perjury.

Two things in that definition do the work. The first is identified by source: potable, nonpotable, recycled, broken out, not aggregated. The second is the split between total and direct, which means a single number off the utility bill does not satisfy the renewal requirement.

One correction worth making, because it has circulated widely: several summaries describe AB 2619 as requiring disclosure of indirect water use, meaning the water consumed generating the site's electricity. The enacted text does not define indirect use and does not require it. If you are scoping a compliance programme, scope it to what the statute says.

What AB 2469 adds, and the 2028 date

AB 2469 operates on the other side of the counter. It applies to cities and counties approving discretionary or ministerial permits for data center construction or expansion that increases maximum peak water use, and it requires a Water Supply Assessment under Water Code section 10910 et seq., projected water use and efficiency measures, workforce disclosures, and an undertaking that the applicant carries the full cost of any water conveyance, treatment, storage or distribution infrastructure the project needs.

Effective 1 January 2028, it also requires a Water Scarcity Plan. That plan has to set out measures for five named conditions: an abnormally dry year, and moderate, severe, extreme and exceptional drought years, including staged reductions, curtailment, recycling and reuse, thermal load reductions, and load shedding.

AB 2469 does not mandate closed-loop cooling. Some coverage says it does. It does not.

The gap this opens

A Water Scarcity Plan is a commitment to cut consumption by a stated amount under stated conditions, written down in advance, in front of a permitting authority. Writing a credible one requires knowing two things that many sites do not currently know with any precision.

The first is where the water is going now, by loop and by source. Evaporative cooling, blowdown, makeup, sanitation and irrigation are different lines with different elasticities, and a site that only knows its total has no basis for saying which it would cut first.

The second is how far each one can be cut before something else breaks. Curtailment on a cooling tower usually means running at higher cycles of concentration: less blowdown, less makeup, and a circuit that is now closer to the scaling and corrosion limits of its own chemistry. Recycling and reuse, both named in the statute, move in the same direction. The water you keep in the loop is water whose composition is drifting.

That is the real operational content of a scarcity plan. It is not a reporting exercise, it is a commitment to run the plant closer to its limits on demand, and the plan is only as good as the site's ability to see what happens when it does.

Where measurement earns its place

Volumes are a flow metering problem, and the renewal report in AB 2619 is largely a question of whether a site is instrumented well enough to break its own consumption apart by source. Many are not, and 2027's renewals will be the first time that shows up with a perjury declaration attached.

Composition is a different problem, and it is the one that decides whether a curtailment commitment is safe to make. A plant running higher cycles, or taking a recycled source that was not in the original design basis, is operating a water chemistry that moves. Spectral change analysis is a reasonable fit here precisely because it does not depend on having a calibrated panel for every constituent that might matter: it watches the spectrum for what is correlating with something the operator cares about, and flags when that relationship moves. BOD is the one parameter AquaMesh calibrates; the rest is change detection.

For sites that already have a few months of history in a historian, the first question is usually answerable from data that exists. What 25 days of one plant's data showed is a reasonable picture of what that kind of look turns up, and it was not a water reporting exercise: it was a cost exercise that happened to require knowing where things actually go.

Nothing in either bill requires a sensor. Both require a site to be able to answer questions about its own water that a surprising number of operators currently answer by estimate. The first renewals under AB 2619 will establish how much tolerance there is for that, and the 2028 scarcity plans will establish how much tolerance there is for a commitment that nobody has tested.

Operators working through what this means for an existing site can see how we approach data center cooling water, or start with an audit of the data already being collected. Understanding what the site's own WUE figure actually measures, and what it omits, is useful context before committing to a curtailment plan; the measurement gap in data center WUE covers that ground.

item.title: What a 25-day historian audit finds at a treatment plant
item.description: A 25-day SCADA export found $42,000/yr in losses at an MBR plant with no site visit. Method, normalized energy benchmarks, and a six-step replication guide.
item.content:encoded:
A 25-day export of a water reuse plant's historian located roughly $42,000 a year in recoverable losses without a site visit, new instruments, or a capital request. The main items were aeration energy running above the plant's own control targets, membrane scour airflow above the manufacturer's specific guidance, and pump cycling at more than twenty times the design rate.

The method is repeatable on any plant with a SCADA or DCS historian: pull an export, locate the parallel equipment pairs, compare each one's performance against the plant's own posted operating ranges, and price every gap that falls outside them. The rest of this post covers that method in detail.

That figure came entirely from the plant's existing SCADA archive: 1,001 tags, 7,172,532 recorded values, covering 28 June to 23 July.

Why a historian export is enough to start

Almost every plant already records far more than anyone reads. A SCADA historian captures every tag on a schedule, forever, and the overwhelming majority of those tags are never looked at unless something breaks. The data is not the constraint. Attention is.

Three properties make that archive useful:

  • It is continuous. A lab result describes one moment. A historian describes every moment, which is the only way to see a slope rather than a point.
  • It contains pairs. Plants run parallel equipment, twin basins, duty and standby pumps, two membrane trains. Equipment built to do the same job under the same conditions should behave the same way. When it stops, that divergence is a measurement in itself.
  • It is already paid for. No capital request, no procurement cycle, no installation window.

The method

For each signal we model what normal looks like for that signal at that plant, rather than against a textbook range. Where the plant publishes its own operating ranges, most do on the weekly sampling schedule, those become the reference. A finding only counts as a finding if it sits outside the range the plant itself posts.

Then each item is priced, which is the part that decides whether anyone acts:

  • Blower power from the isentropic relation, using measured airflow and measured discharge pressure
  • Pump power from measured flow and head
  • Runtime from historian totaliser deltas
  • Everything converted to money using the plant's own tariff

Each line is labelled measured or estimated. Where it is an estimate, the assumptions are written down so the plant's own engineer can check the arithmetic rather than take a vendor's word for it.

Normalizing findings by output

Absolute dollar figures tell you what an opportunity is worth at one plant at one tariff. Normalizing by output tells you whether a plant is already close to its floor or has structural headroom left.

Energy intensity is the standard metric. The EPA's Energy Management Guidebook for Wastewater and Water Utilities benchmarks conventional activated sludge with secondary treatment and UV disinfection at roughly 400 to 1,000 kWh per million gallons treated, depending on nutrient removal requirements. Plants with membrane bioreactors typically run higher, in the range of 2,000 to 4,000 kWh per MG, because continuous air scouring to keep membranes permeable adds a large fixed aeration load that conventional basins do not carry. Plotting a plant's measured intensity on that distribution answers a different question than the dollar figure alone: whether an opportunity is ordinary or exceptional for a plant of that type.

The same logic extends to chemical dosing. Chlorine, polymer, and coagulant dose all should track the flow or load passing through the relevant process step. Dose per unit volume, expressed as mg/L or lb per MG in US customary units, is the trackable metric. A flat chemical dose through wide seasonal flow variation shows up clearly in normalized form. Raw dose data measured in gallons of solution pumped per day hides both overdosing and load-proportional drift.

For the MBR plant in this audit, the actual flow rate is withheld to preserve anonymity. The calculation is the same at any plant: total kWh divided by total volume treated. One month of historian data plus a flow totaliser read is enough to place a plant on the EPA benchmark curve.

What came out

One basin running 3.6x above its own posted range

The plant's sampling schedule posts pre-air dissolved oxygen at 0.5 to 1.5 mg/L. Basin 2 sat right in that band, median 0.49 mg/L. Basin 1 held a median of 5.35 mg/L on every day of the record, roughly eleven times its twin, with its blower command pinned at 99.99%.

Both basins draw on the same shared air header. That detail is what turns this from a mystery into a maintenance task: if the air supply is common and the outcomes are not, the problem is in the split, a valve or a damper, not in the control strategy. Worth $3,316 a year in blower power, plus the nitrogen-removal risk: the EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual identifies dissolved oxygen intrusion into anoxic zones as a primary cause of denitrification inefficiency, since aerobic organisms outcompete denitrifiers at elevated DO concentrations.

One caveat worth repeating: a fouled DO probe can sit on an offset and still respond to airflow changes, making it hard to distinguish a measurement artifact from a real process difference. The reading gets verified against a calibrated handheld before anyone opens a valve. How quickly DO sensors drift in activated sludge mixed liquor, and what calibration intervals are appropriate for that environment, is covered in DO sensor calibration intervals in activated sludge.

Membrane scour air above what the flux needed

Airflow tracked the permeate rate almost perfectly, R-squared of 1.00, at a ratio well above the manufacturer's specific-scour guidance. Trimming toward the guideline at the measured flux, using the controls already installed, came to $5,391 a year. That was the largest no-capital line on the list.

Pumps starting every twenty-five seconds

Reclaimed water pumps were logging 13 to 28 starts an hour against a manufacturer guideline near six for pumps that size. One asset logged 143 in an hour, a start every twenty-five seconds.

Every start draws locked-rotor current and heats the windings far more than running does. The DOE's "Improving Pumping System Performance: A Sourcebook for Industry" documents the relationship between start frequency and insulation aging: permissible starts per hour depend on motor frame size and thermal class, and the typical industrial limit for motors in the fractional to ten-horsepower range is well below what this historian was recording. This is a control deadband adjustment, not a purchase, and it was quietly writing a bill in motors, starters, and contactors: about $3,500 a year.

Sixteen of sixteen reuse totalisers frozen

Every irrigation zone has a volume totaliser. Not one of them changed in twenty-five days.

Until they record, nobody can demonstrate how much recycled water went to beneficial reuse rather than straight to disposal, which is exactly the number a reuse programme is judged on. A configuration fix rather than a purchase, and it unlocks roughly $7,300 a year.

What it added up to

Direct savings, no capital at all$42,050 / yr
Including about 7 h/week of reporting time returned$58,428 / yr
Fully instrumented$92,200 / yr

Two subtotals are kept deliberately apart: money that comes off a bill, and operator hours given back. The hours are real, but they are not money off a bill, so they never get folded into the first number.

How to run this at your plant

The same analysis works on any SCADA or DCS historian export. Six steps:

  1. Pull the export. Three to six weeks covers most seasonal operating modes. IT can usually produce a CSV or Parquet pull from OSIsoft PI, Ignition, or a standard historian without a change request.
  2. Inventory the tags. Group them by equipment and then by process zone. The goal is not to read all 1,000 tags. It is to find the parallel equipment pairs and the flow totalizers.
  3. Find the paired equipment. Twin basins, duty and standby pumps, multiple filters or membrane trains all generate internal comparisons. A performance difference between units drawing on the same feed is a finding with the evidence already in the data. The mechanics of why parallel equipment diverges are covered in why parallel equipment drifts apart.
  4. Check against the plant's own ranges. The sampling schedule or operations manual usually publishes target ranges. A historian signal sitting outside those ranges is a priority flag, because the plant itself told you what normal looks like.
  5. Normalize by output. Divide energy use by treated volume in kWh/MG and chemical dose by treated volume in lb/MG or mg/L. Plot each as a time series. A rising normalized trend over weeks or months indicates process drift that periodic grab sampling will not catch.
  6. Price each finding. Blower and pump power from the isentropic relation or motor-rated amperage; chemical cost from unit price and dose rate; pump starts from the contactor log. Use the plant's own utility tariff. Label measured from estimated.

The sequence takes longer the first time. The second time, most of the work is steps five and six.

The caveat that matters most

Everything above is priced on a residential time-of-use schedule blending to $0.362/kWh. At 406,610 kWh a year this plant is well past residential scale and would normally sit on a commercial schedule at roughly half that blended rate.

On a commercial tariff, the same physical savings are worth about half what is shown.

The kilowatt-hours are measured either way; only their price is in question, and one utility bill settles it. We put that on the front page of the report rather than in a footnote, because showing the range is worth more than picking the flattering end of it.

What this does not tell you

A twenty-five day window in summer will not capture seasonal variation. Capital figures other than instrumentation are order-of-magnitude and need firming with quotes. And every number here is a ceiling that assumes the recommendation is actually implemented and then maintained: an identified opportunity, not a realised saving.

For context on the energy benchmarking side, the wastewater aeration energy cost post covers how to compare blower costs against facility-type benchmarks and what continuous DO monitoring changes about that math.

If your plant keeps a historian, the same exercise is available on your data. It needs an export and nothing else.

Read the full anonymised audit: a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant.

On 28 September 2026, Connect published an announcement about AquaMesh on its blog and through PR distribution. The full release is here: AquaMesh Builds Physical AI to Help Industrial Facilities Catch Costly Problems Early. It also ran on PRLog.

What it covers

The problem. Many plants still find critical problems through delayed lab tests, manual checks, indirect measurements, or alarms that only fire after the problem has already formed. Unplanned industrial downtime is estimated to cost about $260,000 an hour on average.

What AquaMesh does. The platform connects to data a facility already collects and shows where money is being lost. Where a physical or chemical condition can't be measured any other way, it adds its own sensing. From there it works continuously: detect the problem, find the cause, estimate the cost, recommend a response, and check that the response worked.

What it is aiming at. The target is 10% to 25% lower operating cost across water, chemicals, energy, labor and discharge. These are target ranges, not guaranteed results.

Why it matters. In the release, Alex Towfigh describes the core issue as a blind spot about what is physically happening inside a process. Closing it pays off now through production, downtime and operating cost. Over the longer term it is the foundation for facilities that optimize themselves, starting with information operators can trust.

item.title: Why parallel equipment drifts apart, and what the gap costs
item.description: When parallel blowers, pumps or process trains stop matching, something changed. Here is what drives the gap and what it costs.
item.content:encoded:
Parallel blowers and pumps in treatment plants drift apart for three reasons: inlet filter fouling, mechanical wear, and sensor or setpoint mismatch on one unit. Each is fixable. The problem is that the gap produces no control-system alarm. Two basins can sit inside every operating limit while running at completely different airflow rates, and the divergence compounds for months or years undetected.

The cost shows up in three ways: wasted blower electricity, accelerated wear on whichever unit is running harder, and measurement errors that propagate into process and compliance decisions. A basin pair drifting 20 percentage points apart in aeration demand adds hundreds to over a thousand dollars a year in energy alone, before accounting for the wear asymmetry that follows.

The most reliable finding in plant data is also the simplest: two things built to do the same job, under the same conditions, that have stopped behaving the same way.

It is reliable because it needs no baseline, no model of correct operation, and no agreement about what good looks like. The two units are each other's reference. If one has drifted from the other, something changed, and that something usually has a cost attached.

Why the control system will not tell you

A modern control system is very good at holding a value and raising an alarm when a limit is crossed. Divergence between two units is neither of those things.

Both units can sit inside every alarm limit while being nowhere near each other. A pump at 84% duty and its twin at 39% are both running. A basin at 5.35 mg/L and its twin at 0.49 mg/L are both aerated. Nothing is out of range in the sense the alarm system understands, so nothing fires, and the gap persists for years because it never presents as an event.

That is the gap worth watching, and it is visible in data a plant already records.

Neither trace is outside an alarm limit. Both basins are aerated, both are running, and nothing fires.

What drives the gap in blowers and pumps

Blowers drift apart for three main reasons. Inlet filter loading is the most common: as filters accumulate dust, mist and biogenic material, differential pressure rises and actual airflow falls even as the speed command stays the same. Two blowers in the same building foul their filters at different rates depending on position and local airflow patterns. Impeller deposits, particularly from fine aerosols and greasy compounds in municipal treatment plants, shift the speed-to-output curve over years of operation. And control-side drift compounds both effects: a dissolved oxygen sensor reading above actual suppresses the blower command on one basin while its twin continues aerating at a higher level, creating a gap that looks like a mechanical problem until the sensors are checked.

Pumps drift from wear. Return sludge and mixed liquor carry grit that erodes impeller vanes; wear ring clearance grows, and the same speed command delivers progressively less flow. Bearing friction increases as lubrication degrades. Mechanical seals add drag as they age. None of these changes triggers an alarm, but each shifts the relationship between command and output.

Sensor and setpoint mismatch drives divergence on either type of equipment. A dissolved oxygen sensor reading 0.3 mg/L above actual holds one basin's aeration command lower than its twin. A conductivity sensor reading high on a blowdown line, as described in cooling tower blowdown and conductivity drift, opens the blowdown valve beyond what is needed. The control logic on each unit is executing correctly; the gap is upstream of it, in the measurement. How frequently DO sensors drift and what that calibration interval costs in blower energy is covered in DO sensor calibration intervals for activated sludge.

Identifying which cause applies determines the fix: filter cleaning, impeller inspection, or sensor recalibration. The first step is seeing that the gap exists.

The three shapes it takes

Duty that never alternates

Lead and lag assets are supposed to swap. When the alternation is disabled, or was never configured, or was turned off during a commissioning problem and never turned back on, the lead unit accumulates all the wear.

Lead-lag alternation (a standard reliability practice described in the EPA Primer for Municipal Wastewater Treatment Systems) is designed to equalize wear across redundant assets and ensure the standby unit is exercised regularly. The standby that has not run in months is the one the plant will depend on when the lead finally fails.

In one plant's record, return-activated-sludge pumps showed 504 run hours against 232 in the same twenty-five days, and the lifetime counters showed the gap compounding: 44,299 hours against 30,953. The lead unit reaches overhaul years earlier than it needs to while the standby sits idle.

Twenty-five days of run hours, and the lifetime counters behind them.

Lead-lag alternation costs nothing to enable. What makes this finding persuasive rather than theoretical is that the same plant's MBR blowers and permeate pumps were balanced, which marks it as an oversight on one asset rather than a design choice.

A shared supply, unequally split

Twin basins on a common air header should see similar dissolved oxygen at similar load. When one sits far above the other with its blower command pinned wide open, the control strategy is not the problem: the air is not arriving where it is supposed to.

This one is cheap to investigate and cheap to correct, which is what makes it worth finding. A valve position or a damper, not a capital project.

Aeration typically accounts for 55 to 70 percent of a treatment plant's electricity consumption (EPA Energy Management for Water and Wastewater Utilities). An air distribution imbalance between twin basins does not show up in the daily energy report: it shows up in blower run hours, and the cause is upstream of both. How that translates to operating cost is described in aeration energy at wastewater plants.

Instruments that no longer agree

Two turbidimeters on the same permeate stream, one reading a median of 0.11 NTU with a 90th percentile of 0.26, the other reading 0.14 and 2.12: three and a half times the plant's posted upper limit.

One of them is drifting. Until you know which, compliance decisions are resting on an instrument that cannot be fully trusted. The encouraging part, in that case, was that the true value looked excellent.

Dissolved oxygen instruments follow the same pattern. In activated sludge, a DO sensor reading above actual holds the blower on past the setpoint; one reading below actual cuts aeration short before the biology is satisfied. The process consequence of that divergence, particularly during intermittent aeration cycles for nitrogen removal, is covered in intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal.

Why frequent starts cost more than running

A related pattern worth naming on its own, because it is consistently underestimated.

Pumps are often judged on run hours. The more expensive variable is usually starts. Every start draws locked-rotor current several times the running current, and the heat goes into the windings. Motor thermal protection guidelines, as documented in the DOE "Improving Pumping System Performance: A Sourcebook for Industry", establish typical starting limits for mid-size motors because inrush heat cannot dissipate faster than winding insulation allows. Manufacturer specifications typically put that limit at a handful of starts per hour.

In one record, reclaimed water pumps were logging 13 to 28 starts an hour. One asset logged 143 in a single hour: a start every twenty-five seconds. No alarm fired, because at no point was any pump outside its operating limits. It is a control deadband, and the bill arrives years later in motors, starters and contactors.

A modelled scenario puts numbers on that exposure. A 25 hp pump motor rated for 4 starts per hour at full load accumulates locked-rotor heat on each start equivalent to roughly 1 to 2 minutes of continuous running. At 20 starts per hour, the thermal budget that would extend winding life to 8 to 12 years is consumed in 2 to 4 years. A motor rewind at that frame size typically runs $3,000 to $6,000. Annualized across the accelerated interval: $500 to $1,000 per pump per year in a failure mode no process alarm predicted. A facility running four pumps in this pattern carries $2,000 to $4,000 per year in accelerated motor wear, before accounting for starter and contactor replacement at elevated cycle counts.

How to look for it in your own data

You do not need a platform to start. With a historian export and a spreadsheet:

  1. List your parallel assets. Anything with a twin: pumps, blowers, basins, trains, filters.
  2. Compare run hours over the same window, and compare lifetime counters if you have them. A persistent ratio far from 1:1 is the signal.
  3. Count starts per hour, not just runtime, and compare against the manufacturer guidance for that size of machine.
  4. For process variables, plot the pair on the same axis. Not each against its limit: against each other. Divergence that holds for weeks is not noise.
  5. Check duplicates against each other. Two instruments on one stream that disagree are telling you something regardless of which is right.

What you are looking for in every case is persistence. A transient divergence is operations. A divergence that holds for the whole record is a setting, a valve, or an instrument, and all three are fixable.

Why this is where we start

When we read a plant's history, parallel equipment is the first thing modelled, because it produces findings that are concrete, cheap to verify, and hard to argue with. Nobody has to accept a model's opinion about what dissolved oxygen should be. They only have to accept that two basins on the same air header ought to look alike.

item.title: Spectral change analysis versus calibrated parameters
item.description: Most online analysers sell you a parameter list. A spectrum is a different kind of instrument, and pretending otherwise is how vendors end up over-promising. Here is the distinction and why it matters.
item.content:encoded:
An online water quality analyser usually arrives with a list: COD, BOD, TSS, nitrate, TOC. The list is the product. The implication is that the instrument measures each of those things the way a lab measures them, only continuously.

That is not how spectral measurement works, and the gap between how it is sold and how it behaves is where a lot of disappointment comes from.

What the instrument actually produces

A UV/Vis probe does one thing: it measures how much light the water absorbs across a range of wavelengths, many times a second. What comes back is a curve, an absorbance spectrum. That curve is the raw measurement. Everything else is interpretation.

Converting that curve into "COD = 212 mg/L" requires a model that maps spectral shape to a lab value. Such models exist, they can be built, and for some parameters on some streams they are good. ISO 15839, which sets performance specifications for online water quality analysers, addresses this directly: models must be validated for the specific application, and performance characteristics may vary by site. In practice, this means the conditions that worked at one plant do not transfer automatically:

  • They are often site-specific. Transferability must be demonstrated; a model validated on one stream should not be assumed valid on another.
  • They drift with composition. Change the recipe, the season, the raw material or the upstream process, and the relationship between spectrum and lab value moves.
  • They degrade quietly. A calibration that has stopped being right does not announce it. It keeps producing plausible numbers.

Without reference checks and maintenance, a parameter model can keep producing plausible numbers after its error has grown.

The alternative: watch the spectrum move

There is a different use of the same hardware, and in a plant it is usually the more valuable one.

Instead of asking what is the concentration, ask has the fingerprint changed, and what does that change correlate with. Build a one-time model of what the plant's own stream normally looks like. Then watch for deviation from that reference, and tie the deviation to what the plant was doing at the time: feed rate, wash flow, machine state, cleaning records.

This is a materially easier question to answer well, and it is insensitive to the things that break calibrations:

  • It does not need an absolute value, so it does not need to hold an absolute calibration
  • It can handle defined operating modes more transparently when each recipe or season has an appropriate reference; new conditions still need review
  • A drifting baseline shows up as drift rather than as a wrong number presented confidently

{{diagram:calibration-vs-change}} Same hardware, same spectrum, two different questions. Two very different maintenance burdens.

What you lose is the ability to report a concentration to a regulator. What you gain is a clear operating signal whose performance can be checked against current references over time.

So why calibrate BOD at all

Because sometimes a number is the point.

Biochemical oxygen demand is the parameter that drives sewer surcharges, appears in discharge permits under 40 CFR Part 133, and determines whether a load is going to cause a problem downstream. "The spectrum moved" is not an answer when the question is whether you are about to exceed a threshold that gets billed by the pound.

For the first industrial deployment, BOD is the parameter we plan to validate against the customer's own reference samples. The reference test is Standard Method 5210B, as codified in 40 CFR Part 136. Their lab stays the method of record. The goal is to fill the hours between the samples the lab already takes, rather than replace them.

Other outputs begin as change analysis unless and until they are validated against an appropriate reference method.

Why be this specific about it

Partly because it is true, and a claim that is not true gets found out in a technical review.

But mostly because the honest version is a better product story. "We measure sixteen parameters" invites a comparison against instruments from companies with thirty years of calibration work behind them, on a spec sheet, where we would lose. "We watch the whole spectrum for change and tell you what it correlates with in your plant, and we plan to validate BOD against your lab" is a different claim, and a parameter list does not answer it.

It also sets expectations that survive deployment. An operator who was told they were getting continuous COD and finds the number drifting stops trusting the instrument. An operator who was told they were getting an early warning that something in the water changed, and gets exactly that, keeps using it.

What this means in practice

For a plant considering continuous optical measurement, three questions are worth asking any vendor:

  1. Which parameters are calibrated against my samples, and which are inferred? The answer should be short and specific.
  2. What happens to the calibration when my feedstock changes? If the answer is vague, assume it drifts.
  3. What is the instrument useful for if I never calibrate anything? A good spectral instrument still earns its place as a change detector. A repackaged parameter list does not.

Where this sits in the stack

Measurement is only half of it. A spectrum that moved is not an action: it becomes useful when it is correlated with plant state, attributed to a unit, and priced.

That is the division of labour: the probe reads the stream, the platform works out what the change means and what it is worth, and the operator decides what to do about it. What that process looks like against a real plant dataset is in what 25 days of historian data actually shows. Working from a production historian to find cost events is the practical version of the correlation step described above.
